posts.title: At $1,950 an ounce, annual primary supply is worth about $2 billion. Miners have little scope to increase production as demand grows. Add a chemical recovery to the long-term growth in electronics, and the shortage gets harder to fill. Ruthenium to the moon! (5/5)

Demand already exceeds supply, even with chemicals, its largest end market, in a downturn. Johnson Matthey expects demand of 1.193 million ounces against primary supply of 977,000 ounces in 2026. Chemical demand is forecast to fall 16%, largely because Chinese nylon producers have built too much capacity. That weakness helps explain why the price has not risen further. Some producers have switched catalysts, but chemical demand has recovered from past downturns, and we expect another recovery. Electronics demand grew from 300,000 ounces in 2023 to 413,000 in 2025, with 435,000 forecast for 2026. Datacenter expansion is expected to lift ruthenium demand in hard drives to a five-year high this year. Conventional drives use small amounts of the metal, so higher prices add little to their cost. We expect datacenter storage to keep expanding and new chip applications to accelerate ruthenium demand. A recovery in chemicals would add to that growth. (4/5)

Higher prices give miners little reason to produce more ruthenium. Most comes from South African platinum mines, where it is recovered as a byproduct. It accounted for just 3.3% of Sibanye-Stillwater's platinum group metal revenue in 2025, so mining plans still depend chiefly on the other metals in the ore. Primary supply was about 30 tonnes that year, down 14% because the release of producer inventories in 2024 was not repeated. Inventories have covered the gap between supply and demand in recent years. (3/5)

As chip wiring shrinks, the layers that stop copper from spreading into surrounding materials take up more of the wire. Ruthenium can work without copper's diffusion-barrier stack, and its resistivity rises less sharply as the wire narrows. At widths around 17nm and below, it can compete with copper. It also melts more than 1,000°C above copper and expands less than half as much when heated, reducing the mismatch with silicon. These properties make it a leading candidate to replace copper in the narrowest wires in chips beyond 2nm. Ruthenium already helps copper wiring scale through its use in liners. Researchers have also demonstrated ruthenium-filled nano-TSVs, or through-silicon vias: tiny vertical connections that can deliver power from the back of a chip. Imec has separately demonstrated ruthenium buried power rails. (2/5)

Ruthenium has risen from about $560 an ounce in early 2025 to dealer quotes near $1,950 this September. It is a key material in hard drives, with new use cases also emerging. (1/5)🧵 https://t.co/WvdZq5Y1ov

posts.title: Democrats are trying to dismiss the White House Accord on Super Intelligence as optional self-policing. But although the agreement was entered into voluntarily, the governance that follows from it is not. As Gavin Baker points out, once an independent auditor reports a safety issue to an independent board committee, directors have a fiduciary duty not to disregard it, and a D&O carrier can use a bad-faith finding to deny coverage. So although the agreement starts with internal controls, these are verified by external audit and board oversight — and then existing FTC and securities law still apply to any public claim the company does not keep. This is far more practical than what Democrats want — a freeze on frontier development while China races ahead. Democrats should applaud what President Trump has accomplished. But they would rather use SI safety as a campaign issue than admit the Accord represents major progress.
